scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.
evidence.value_checked: gate:http_envelope | PASS on all 40 relations, envelope + status agree with body | probes live as anon / member / no-key, error bodies included | 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence (PostgREST+RLS by construction), each answered at the page layer: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1 | depends_on: project-report.html, tools/prove_http_envelope.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.
evidence.value_checked: gate:http_envelope | PASS: status agrees with body on all 40 relations | probed live as anon / member / no-key | 27 relations structurally cannot separate refusal from absence (PostgREST+RLS), answered per page: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1 | depends_on: project-report.html, tools/prove_http_envelope.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.
evidence.value_checked: gate:read_idempotency | 93 repeatable reads across 22 pages, PASS | idempotent 83, uncontrolled 5, modulo-clock 2, control-failed 2, unknown 1 | digest proven sensitive | depends_on: project-report.html, tools/prove_read_idempotency.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.
evidence.value_checked: gate:paginated-order-totality | 176 chains scanned, 0 non-total, forward-only PASS | selftest both directions | caught+fixed this session: report-sender.html:1357 order(triggered_at) | depends_on: project-report.html, tools/validate_paginated_order_totality.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the value carries its unit at the boundary (pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent) - the class that made a knob of 10 mean 1000%

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.detail: MEASURED AND FAILING - the edge layer's error envelope is not machine-readable, and it is not shaped like the db layer's. Two concrete defects, both measured against the local edge runtime this session: (1) an edge function's error body is {"error": "<prose>"} with NO machine-readable `code` field, so a caller can only pattern-match English to decide what happened - while the SAME platform's db layer returns {code, details, hint, message} for every failure class (400 bad column, 404 unknown table, 401 no grant), which a client CAN branch on. One product, two incompatible error contracts. (2) a routing 404 (unknown function name) is returned as **text/plain**, so `res.json()` THROWS rather than yielding an error object - the caller's catch block sees a SyntaxError about unexpected token, not a 404, and any code that checks `data.error` never runs. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: this is the layer behind the AI gateway, the orchestrators, OCR/voice capture and report generation. A client that treats db and edge errors alike - which the identical-looking `.error` property invites - will mishandle one of them, and the failure mode is the one this bank keeps finding: an exception swallowed into an empty render, indistinguishable from a server that honestly answered nothing. LEFT OWED RATHER THAN GREEN, DELIBERATELY: the oracle asks that status and body AGREE and that the envelope be uniform, and it does not. Banking it green would be a false green; recording it owed with the diagnosis is the honest state. TO FINISH: return JSON for routing 404s (Content-Type application/json), and add a stable `code` alongside `error` in every edge error body, then re-walk. That is an edge-function change and belongs in a batched wave, not mid-walk.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. evidence.asserts: What one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS: a value is not silently rewritten on the way in by something nobody named. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - values_survive_write extracts every trigger that assigns to NEW, classifies the rewrite by its STRUCTURE, and fails on any that belongs to no named class. It also measures the one class that can lose a person's work: every left(NEW.col, N) cap is read against the stored data, because a possible truncation and an actual one are different facts.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). It earned that by first FAILING on a trigger I had added earlier in this same session: tg_community_posts_moderation_fields, which restores flagged/pinned for a caller who is not a supervisor of that hive (migrations ...000063/64, after a reported author was found clearing their own flag). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. The fix was to teach the CLASSIFIER a new structural class, field-authorization-guard, not to rename my trigger guard_* to slip past a prefix check: the function's own docstring says widening the name allowlist until the gate goes green is bending the gate, and structure is what a rewrite DOES. The new class is detected on shape - every assignment restoring the column to its own prior value - so no outside value replaces the caller's and their other edits still land.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_null_semantics.py - 286 client coalesce sites read out of the pages and joined against the SCHEMA, so each one is judged against whether its column can actually be NULL. ★THE ORACLE'S OWN EXAMPLE IS NUMERIC: 'NULL meant no cap in the DB and arrived as a cap of ZERO in the client'. So the sites are separated by what the substitution DESTROYS, not by how many there are: numeric-substitute (50) and boolean-substitute (3) turn an UNKNOWN into a definite value and are the real class; not-null-in-db (15) cannot fire because the column is NOT NULL; visible-placeholder (47) renders an em-dash or equivalent and is the CORRECT behaviour, not a defect; text-blank (171) collapses NULL to '' where both already render as nothing - a weaker concern, recorded but not charged as this oracle's failure. ★THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A REAL NULL, which is what stops a clean page from being a vacuous pass: the control column v_achievement_xp_log.source_id holds 77 live NULLs and is found. A detector that cannot see that cannot see any. ★AND THE LIVE COUNT IS SEPARATE FROM THE LATENT ONE: zero of these sites is misbehaving TODAY, because the columns concerned currently hold no NULLs (0/4, 0/95, 0/97 on the ones sampled). That is a fact about this dataset, not about the code - which is precisely why the structural reading is the one banked here, and why 'no NULL has appeared yet' is not recorded as safety. findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_null_semantics.py - 286 client coalesce sites read out of the pages and joined against the SCHEMA, so each one is judged against whether its column can actually be NULL. ★THE ORACLE'S OWN EXAMPLE IS NUMERIC: 'NULL meant no cap in the DB and arrived as a cap of ZERO in the client'. So the sites are separated by what the substitution DESTROYS, not by how many there are: numeric-substitute (50) and boolean-substitute (3) turn an UNKNOWN into a definite value and are the real class; not-null-in-db (15) cannot fire because the column is NOT NULL; visible-placeholder (47) renders an em-dash or equivalent and is the CORRECT behaviour, not a defect; text-blank (171) collapses NULL to '' where both already render as nothing - a weaker concern, recorded but not charged as this oracle's failure. ★THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A REAL NULL, which is what stops a clean page from being a vacuous pass: the control column v_achievement_xp_log.source_id holds 77 live NULLs and is found. A detector that cannot see that cannot see any. ★AND THE LIVE COUNT IS SEPARATE FROM THE LATENT ONE: zero of these sites is misbehaving TODAY, because the columns concerned currently hold no NULLs (0/4, 0/95, 0/97 on the ones sampled). That is a fact about this dataset, not about the code - which is precisely why the structural reading is the one banked here, and why 'no NULL has appeared yet' is not recorded as safety. FOR THIS PAGE: 5 site(s) substitute a definite value for a possibly-NULL column, which is the exact shape this oracle names. Example: `i.pct_complete || 0` - column `pct_complete` (smallint), nullable on v_project_items_truth,v_project_progress, so an UNKNOWN would arrive as 0. Not misbehaving today only because those columns currently hold no NULLs, which is a property of the data and not of the code.

evidence.asserts: What one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS: a value is not silently rewritten on the way in by something nobody named. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - values_survive_write extracts every trigger that assigns to NEW, classifies the rewrite by its STRUCTURE, and fails on any that belongs to no named class. It also measures the one class that can lose a person's work: every left(NEW.col, N) cap is read against the stored data, because a possible truncation and an actual one are different facts.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). It earned that by first FAILING on a trigger I had added earlier in this same session: tg_community_posts_moderation_fields, which restores flagged/pinned for a caller who is not a supervisor of that hive (migrations ...000063/64, after a reported author was found clearing their own flag). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. The fix was to teach the CLASSIFIER a new structural class, field-authorization-guard, not to rename my trigger guard_* to slip past a prefix check: the function's own docstring says widening the name allowlist until the gate goes green is bending the gate, and structure is what a rewrite DOES. The new class is detected on shape - every assignment restoring the column to its own prior value - so no outside value replaces the caller's and their other edits still land.

findings.title: QUALIFIED: with 7 reads answered 500 this page DOES speak up - 'This project could not be loaded. It may have been removed, or you may not have access.' - and asserts no number, which is most of what the oracle asks. It is recorded as a finding rather than a pass because **the diagnosis is wrong**.
findings.detail: QUALIFIED: with 7 reads answered 500 this page DOES speak up - 'This project could not be loaded. It may have been removed, or you may not have access.' - and asserts no number, which is most of what the oracle asks. It is recorded as a finding rather than a pass because **the diagnosis is wrong**. A 500 IS NOT A PERMISSION PROBLEM AND NOT A DELETION. Telling a reader the project 'may have been removed, or you may not have access' during a transport fault sends them to ask an administrator for access they already hold, or to conclude a live project was deleted. This is the 401-vs-403 class already recorded on this platform: two different events must not share one sentence, because the recovery actions differ - wait and retry, versus request access, versus accept a deletion. TO FINISH: branch on the error. A 5xx says 'we could not reach the server, try again'; a 403 says 'you do not have access to this project'; an empty result says 'this project no longer exists'. The page already has the error object - `utils.js` carries `whIsAuthFailure` / `whWriteError` for exactly this split, so it is adoption rather than new code. MEASURED BY ANSWERING EVERY READ WITH A 500 AT window.fetch AND READING WHAT THE PAGE SAYS NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request resolves to a synthetic `{"code":"500"}` with Content-Type application/json; `/auth/v1/` is untouched so the session survives, which is what makes this a SERVER fault rather than a dead network. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. Every claim below quotes the page's own visible sentence, collected from leaf-ish elements under a composed-visibility test (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) so hidden template copy cannot be mistaken for something a reader sees. TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS SWEEP WERE THROWN AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE NUMBERS HERE ARE TRUSTED. The first used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered live data - a registered service worker sits between page and transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. The second omitted the identity guard and returned byte-identical output for seven different pages (14,677 chars of marketing copy) because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. This version guards INSIDE the evaluate: expected uid, `location.pathname` ends in the page's own file, and body chars outside the 13,000-16,000 landing band - refusing rather than reporting. PLATFORM RESULT, all 22 pages: **9 state the failure in domain language** (hive, inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, index, skillmatrix, achievements, voice-journal, assistant) and **11 say nothing or assert a falsehood**. Only 2 offer a retry CONTROL (achievements, community); public-feed's was measured firing a real re-request and rendering 15 posts.

findings.detail: FAILS: 8 call(s) failed and the page said NOTHING about it (1167 chars healthy -> 1167 chars failed). THE ORACLE IS A DIFFERENCE, NOT A STRING, inherited from the marketplace spec this extends: the page is read HEALTHY first, and a pass requires the failure wording to APPEAR - if the healthy render already said it, the words were always there and prove nothing, so the page is UNGRADED. A pass therefore means the page answered a broken read with something failure-shaped that it does not say when healthy. FOUR WAYS TO FAIL IT: rendering EMPTINESS ('no items', 'nothing here') for a failure - the two are indistinguishable to a person and one of them is a lie, and this platform shipped exactly that when public-feed's Retry answered 'No public posts yet' over 15 existing posts; leaving a SKELETON shimmering at someone whose data will never arrive; saying nothing at all; or being ungraded because the injection never fired. The vocabulary is IMPORTED from session_signals.mjs, harvested from this product's own sentences - the spec's own note is that an oracle recognising only its author's phrasing measures vocabulary, not behaviour. ★ THREE OF THE SEVEN MODES CARRY THEIR OWN PASS CONDITION, because 'did a failure message appear?' is the right question for only four of them, and using one assertion for all seven is how a family looks green while asserting the wrong thing on three of its members. fail_slow is a SUCCESSFUL read that is merely late: demanding a failure message there would be demanding a LIE. It must show the page is WORKING - a skeleton, spinner or busy state - and it is sampled MID-FLIGHT, at 2.5s of a 6s delay, because by the time the data lands the answer has been erased; a final-state read would score a page that showed a blank screen for six seconds identically to one that showed a skeleton. fail_null_field is not an error at all - the rows arrive and their non-id fields are null - so the only question is whether the page prints `null`, `undefined` or `NaN` at a person. The nulls are applied to the REAL response rather than to a synthesised one, so the test exercises the page's own schema instead of this prover's idea of it, and the match is word-bounded so 'Nullarbor' or a part code containing 'nan' cannot trip it. fail_partial is a 200 whose JSON does not parse - what a connection dropped mid-transfer actually looks like - and must read as a failure rather than as 'no rows'. WHAT THE NULL MODE ACTUALLY FOUND, verified page by page rather than inferred from a sweep line: three pages print a raw null at a person, and all three share ONE shape - a `|| fallback` present on one interpolation and missing on its NEIGHBOUR in the same template literal. inventory:1542 `Available: ${item.qty_on_hand} ${item.unit || 'pcs'}` renders OUT OF STOCK null pcs eight times: the UNIT fell back, the QUANTITY did not - the page guards the decoration and leaves the number a technician acts on unguarded. alert-hub:611 `shift ${brief.shift_date} · model ${brief.model_version || 'amc-v1'}` prints `shift null` while rendering `(no headline)` two lines later, so the idiom was in hand at the time. skillmatrix:854 `Primary: ${_profile.primary_skill} · ${WORKER_NAME}` prints `Primary: null · Leandro Marquez` - a raw null in a person's DISCIPLINE, beside their name, on the surface whose job is stating their qualifications. THE CONSEQUENCES DIFFER AND ARE NOT FLATTENED: a wrong quantity, a wrong claim about a person, a wrong shift on a supervisor's brief. One habit, three one-token corrections - not a design decision. HOW THE FAILURE IS INDUCED, and why the method is the hard part: every Supabase REST/RPC call is failed at window.fetch, patched via addInitScript so it is in place BEFORE any page script runs. That timing is the whole trick. tests/failure-injection.spec.ts records that replacing window.fetch AFTER load never fires, because supabase-js captures fetch when the CLIENT IS CONSTRUCTED - so it used page.route instead; this project separately learned that page.route is bypassed by a warm SERVICE WORKER serving from cache. Both are true, and the reconciliation is WHEN THE PATCH LANDS: an init script is not a late override, and it sits above the service worker rather than below it. THE INJECTION COUNTS ITS OWN HITS and a page where the counter reads zero is UNGRADED, never judged - because a failure-injection oracle that does not inject produces the most convincing false findings available: 'the page said nothing about the error' is exactly what a page with NO error would say. WHAT THIS ORACLE FOUND ON ITS FIRST RUN, and it was a hole in a fix made earlier the same day: the central transport notice hung off `.then(res => ...)`, so a REJECTED or ABORTED fetch - which never produces a res - skipped it entirely. Status-bearing failures (500/401) were covered; transport failures were not. Measured on logbook: 13 rejected reads, ZERO page errors, ZERO console errors, and not one word on screen - the page caught the rejection and dropped it, which is the '118 annotated empty-catch blocks across 11 pages' habit utils.js already documents. FIXED at the transport in a `.catch` that NOTICES AND RE-THROWS, because that wrapper's own comment forbids a catch that swallows the error callers must surface; `throw err` leaves every caller's {data, error} untouched. scenarios.question: the cross-layer facts about THIS page that must hold at every instant, asserted from the source of truth rather than from a screen
scenarios.oracle: a foreign hive's projects are invisible

evidence.asserts: a foreign hive's projects are invisible
evidence.checked: PASSES. The platform's live two-tenant isolation gate reports 26 pass / 0 fail, and this page's claim is one it covers directly: a member of one hive reaches ZERO rows of another hive's data through the read path, and a spoofed attribution on a write is rebound to the caller. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of the 26 invariants returning a row it should not - and the gate is known to fire, because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught (1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker). HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the gate that already exists rather than writing another one: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. It reports 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS A ROLE-CORRECT PROBE, which is what makes it worth anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims, because a probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction. The actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot silently turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the wrong reason and read as a pass. WHAT IT ACTUALLY ASSERTS, in its own terms: a foreign hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows (the defect that once leaked 1,105 rows of another tenant's logbook to a non-member, caused by views missing security_invoker so they ran as superuser and bypassed base RLS); membership cannot be self-joined or restored after a kick; and a spoofed submitter on an INSERT is server-pinned to the caller across logbook, asset_nodes, projects, pm_assets, pm_completions, community_posts, community_replies, inventory_items, engineering_calcs, parts_records and voice_journal_entries. It also carries no-regression checks, so a gate that passed by breaking the legitimate path would be caught. SCOPE LIMIT, ENFORCED RATHER THAN MENTIONED: this evidence is a DATABASE proof. Any oracle on this platform that also asserts isolation 'through the realtime channel' makes a second claim that psql cannot reach, and every such row was deliberately LEFT OWED by this banker instead of being settled on half a proof. Banking them here would be the exact shape of an oracle that does not match its claim.
evidence.value_checked: hive isolation gate: 26 pass / 0 fail, live two-tenant, rolled back

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 5 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

Most numbers on this platform are COUNTS - 9 open jobs, 28 PMs overdue - and a count has no unit to show; flagging those would redden every surface, and a check that reddens everything is measuring itself. So 'MTBF: 45' fails, 'MTBF: 45 days' passes, and 'Open Jobs: 9' is never asked. ★THIS VIEW RENDERED ZERO DIMENSION-LABELLED QUANTITIES ON ITS DEFAULT STATE, so the check ABSTAINS rather than passing. (1) It first accepted only BARE digits, so any value already carrying its unit never entered the set - 21 of 22 pages reported '0 judged' on a platform that renders MTBF and OEE nearly everywhere. An implausible abstention is an instrument fault, not a finding. (2) It then failed analytics on 'total downtime = 717.9h' because the time vocabulary listed hr/hrs/hours but not a bare 'h'. An oracle's vocabulary IS the oracle. Both are fixed and recorded in the tool. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: drive this page's V2/V3 views open before scanning - the quantities that owe units here live behind a modal, a tab or a selected record, exactly as effect_visible needed the disclosure and the selection performed before it could see anything.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 7 reads answered 500, **no retry control is present** - zero visible elements whose label mentions retry or try-again. It offers 'Back to Project Manager' - a navigation escape rather than a retry, so the failed read is never re-attempted. SO THE ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant costs the whole page again on the connection that just failed. THE PATTERN EXISTS ON THIS PLATFORM, so this is adoption: achievements renders a Retry button beside its toast, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 post cards. Only 2 of 22 pages have one. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that RE-ISSUES the failed read - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY ANSWERING EVERY READ WITH A 500 AT window.fetch AND READING WHAT THE PAGE SAYS NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request resolves to a synthetic `{"code":"500"}` with Content-Type application/json; `/auth/v1/` is untouched so the session survives, which is what makes this a SERVER fault rather than a dead network. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. Every claim below quotes the page's own visible sentence, collected from leaf-ish elements under a composed-visibility test (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) so hidden template copy cannot be mistaken for something a reader sees. TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS SWEEP WERE THROWN AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE NUMBERS HERE ARE TRUSTED. The first used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered live data - a registered service worker sits between page and transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. The second omitted the identity guard and returned byte-identical output for seven different pages (14,677 chars of marketing copy) because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. This version guards INSIDE the evaluate: expected uid, `location.pathname` ends in the page's own file, and body chars outside the 13,000-16,000 landing band - refusing rather than reporting. PLATFORM RESULT, all 22 pages: **9 state the failure in domain language** (hive, inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, index, skillmatrix, achievements, voice-journal, assistant) and **11 say nothing or assert a falsehood**. Only 2 offer a retry CONTROL (achievements, community); public-feed's was measured firing a real re-request and rendering 15 posts.

findings.title: MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean.
findings.detail:
MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean. ★THE INDUCTION IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, which is the difference between a verdict and a guess: the lens reports inductionLanded, the number of reads that actually went out under the injected condition, and refuses to score a page that never re-queried. Its own comment records why - it once read retry_path:false / fallback:silentlyStale on a surface that handles both correctly, because closure-scoped loaders meant the page never moved, and it scored the UNCHANGED page. Every verdict banked here carries inductionLanded > 0 and inconclusive:false. ★AND THE LENS IS PROVEN ABLE TO PASS, so a FAIL is not a blanket instrument failure: across the roster it returned retry_path 3 PASS / 19 FAIL, rate_limit_legible 1/21, fallback_engaged 7/15, slow_honest 10/12. public-feed passes all four - consistent with its own history, since it is the page fixed so a failed read renders an error rather than 'No public posts yet'. RETRY PATH - FAILS, and the half that is certain is the half that matters. Under an injected 500 this page offers ZERO retry affordances: no 'try again', no 'reload', no 'refresh' control. That is confirmed TWO independent ways - the lens counted affordances:0, and a separate direct probe that 500'd every /rest/v1/ request and scanned the whole document for a retry control also found none. A person whose data failed to load has nothing to press. ★ONE HALF OF THIS VERDICT IS INSTRUMENT-DEPENDENT AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH RATHER THAN BANKED AS FACT: the lens also reported saysFailure:False. My direct probe, which failed EVERY read rather than the subset the lens induces, and which scanned the whole page rather than <main>, found that this page DOES say something failed under a total outage. So the page's failure MESSAGING may be better than the lens's number suggests - a partial induction can leave a surface half-populated and quiet. The missing retry CONTROL is not in doubt; the missing failure SENTENCE is, on this page. WHY IT IS NOT BANKED GREEN ANYWAY: the oracle asks for a retry PATH, and a failure a person cannot act on is the shape this family exists to catch - 'a failure that offers a retry which does not re-attempt is worse than one that offers none', and offering none at all is the floor of that same scale.

★RETRACTED CONTEXT ON THIS ROW'S RECORDED TALLY: it lists rate_limit_legible as 1P/21F. That figure is true of THIS LENS and misleading about the platform, and is retracted as evidence of any gap. 42 rate_limit_legible rows are banked green on a 2026-08-09 induction against the REAL limit - 400 logbook inserts inside BEGIN...ROLLBACK as an authenticated member, refused with 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' plus HINT logbook_daily_user, and a second hive-tier quota at SQLSTATE 54000 that states its remedy. THE PLATFORM'S RATE LIMITING IS LEGIBLE. This lens asked a different question - whether a page's TEXT names a limit under a FAKE 429 injected at the fetch layer, a client-rendering question about a condition the server never produced. PRECEDENCE (roadmap 6l/6m): a prover that induced the REAL condition outranks a lens that simulated one; the disagreement is scope, never regression. THE VERDICT ON THIS ROW'S OWN KEY IS UNAFFECTED - it rests on its own induction, which landed (inductionLanded > 0).

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.

findings.detail: NOT MEASURED - THE SURFACE WAS NOT ARRIVED AT, and recording that is the point. project-report requires a `?project_id=` parameter to render a report; without it the page is a shell, and this probe loaded it bare. The reading it produced (5 reads in flight, 0 server-derived writes, 0 skeletons) would have banked as a clean pass while measuring almost nothing - the flattering-zero trap that has already produced three false readings in this arc (asset-hub with no asset, analytics-report before Generate, project-report without project_id - this very page). TO FINISH: load `project-report.html?project_id=853abed7-4a61-4bb4-b771-f0d2d0196490` (a real CAP-2026-001 project in the test hive), then re-run the delayed-read probe. The arrival is one URL parameter, so this is a one-call unit rather than a blocker.

evidence.asserts: a slow read is shown as slow - the page never answers with a server-derived value it does not have yet
evidence.checked: PASSES, AND THE ARRIVAL IS PART OF THE EVIDENCE. An earlier pass loaded this page bare and got a clean-looking reading over a 363-character shell; that reading was WITHHELD rather than banked, because project-report renders nothing without a `?project_id=`. This run loaded `project-report.html?project_id=853abed7-4a61-4bb4-b771-f0d2d0196490` (CAP-2026-001 in the test hive) and the surface reached **4,124 characters** - so the denominator is real. MEASURED: 9 reads in flight, **0 server-derived writes**, 4 skeleton elements and explicit loading vocabulary on screen. After the reads resolved, 42 numeric writes landed - `kpi-value` = 64%, 0 and 4. So every figure waited for its data, and the page said it was working while they did. MEASURED BY DETECTING THE WRITE, WITH A POSITIVE CONTROL. Reads are wrapped in a 5s delay and counted on resolution; a MutationObserver records every mutation whose text is purely numeric, stamped with how many reads had resolved at that moment - so 'did the page write a number before it had the data?' is a measured fact. The probe writes its own sentinel ('4242') and the reading is REFUSED unless the observer sees it; every page in this wave returned controlOK = true. THE CONTROL EXISTS BECAUSE TWO EARLIER VERSIONS LIED IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION - one tested only the added node's own text (missing numeric leaves inside an innerHTML render), the other never attached because `document.documentElement` was null at init-script time. Both reported 0 writes on pages that visibly populated. THE ORACLE IS 'were SERVER-DERIVED numbers written', not 'were numbers written': writes to the local offline-queue badge (`wh-conn-queue`, an IndexedDB depth needing no read), decorative stage numerals and engineering-design's static catalogue `pill-count` are classified separately and excluded.

findings.title: CLASSIFIED WITH EVIDENCE rather than left un-attempted.
findings.detail: CLASSIFIED WITH EVIDENCE rather than left un-attempted. This oracle asks that offline the write be REFUSED before firing and the person told nothing was sent - so before it can be graded, this view's committing write has to be identified and its CLASS settled, because the platform deliberately splits them: field capture QUEUES, while approvals, locked, financial, moderation and role writes are online-only-with-clarity (the generic drain carries no optimistic lock and those writes depend on one). Grading a queue-backed write against a refusal is wrong in both directions - green credits a refusal that must not exist, red calls a working feature a defect. The test is per-FUNCTION, not per-page: inventory, community and skillmatrix each show BOTH classes on one page. See PAGE_TESTBANK_ROADMAP.md SS6 for the sibling offline_queued cell proposed for the queue side, and tools/prove_offline_queued.mjs which grades it. THIS VIEW HAS NO COMMITTING WRITE. a grep for .insert/.update/.upsert/.delete across the whole page returns ZERO - this is a read-and-generate surface, and the budget block reads through get_project_budget, an RPC the page never writes with. So the oracle has nothing to grade, and a green would be a pass over an empty denominator - the false green this bank exists to prevent. It is not declared-na either: R10 wants a reason AND a replacement, and the honest replacement is that the report's figures equal project-manager's for the same project, and that a failed read is visible as a failure rather than a zeroed budget - CD invariant 1 and CC fail_offline, which belongs to other cells rather than this one.

Six pages passing is what separates 'nobody built this' from 'not every read path routes through it'. FOR THIS PAGE THE FINDING IS DIFFERENT AND MORE SERIOUS, so it is NOT scored as a retry problem. Under a TOTAL read outage the page renders no failure at all - nothing says anything went wrong. A retry has nothing to attach to until the page first admits the failure, and a surface that stays quiet while every read fails is the stuck-skeleton/false-empty class this bank exists to catch. findings.detail: NOT MEASURED - THE SURFACE WAS NOT ARRIVED AT, and recording that is the point. project-report requires a `?project_id=` parameter to render a report; without it the page is a shell, and this probe loaded it bare. The reading it produced (5 reads in flight, 0 server-derived writes, 0 skeletons) would have banked as a clean pass while measuring almost nothing - the flattering-zero trap that has already produced three false readings in this arc (asset-hub with no asset, analytics-report before Generate, project-report without project_id - this very page). TO FINISH: load `project-report.html?project_id=853abed7-4a61-4bb4-b771-f0d2d0196490` (a real CAP-2026-001 project in the test hive), then re-run the delayed-read probe. The arrival is one URL parameter, so this is a one-call unit rather than a blocker.

evidence.asserts: a slow read is shown as slow IN THIS VIEW - it never answers with a server-derived value it does not have yet
evidence.checked: WHY THIS ROW WAS RE-MEASURED. Its previous evidence was IDENTICAL to the V1 row's on the same page - a KPI-tile reading taken at page load - because the banking loop selected rows by oracle name and swept both views with one page-level measurement. Fourteen V2 rows across the platform carried a measurement of a view they never visited, which is R7's exact failure: a claim resting on something other than what it names. The count did not move; the evidence did. PASSES, on an ARRIVED surface. The page was loaded as `project-report.html?project_id=853abed7-4a61-4bb4-b771-f0d2d0196490` (CAP-2026-001 in the test hive), because without a project_id this page is a 363-char shell and a reading over it would be the flattering-zero trap. With 9 reads in flight and 0 resolved, **0 numeric writes landed inside the report containers** and `#exec-summary` held **4 skeleton elements**. STATED PRECISELY: the budget block's own container is not in the DOM while the reads pend - the report renders its sections after data arrives - so what is proven is that no budget figure is asserted early, not that a budget skeleton exists. MEASURED WITH THE DELAY ARMED AFTER INITIAL LOAD, which is what makes a V2 view measurable at all. A modal or thread cannot be opened while the feed that renders its opener is still pending, so the fetch wrapper starts INERT and is armed only once the page has settled; the view is then opened and its OWN read is the one held in flight. Every reading below is refused unless `resolved === 0` at measurement time and at least one request was intercepted, so neither a vacuous run nor an already-resolved one can be reported as a pass. AND WHERE NUMERIC WRITES ARE COUNTED, THEY ARE ATTRIBUTED BY CONTAINMENT: each write's ancestor chain is walked and only writes landing INSIDE this view's container count, so a page-level write cannot credit or convict the wrong view. The observer writes its own '4242' sentinel and the reading is REFUSED unless it sees it - a control that refused this very batch once, when the config was passed to the MutationObserver constructor instead of observe(), so observe() threw and the observer silently never attached. An unattached observer reports zero writes on every page.

scenarios.oracle: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible

evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: member (tenant boundary) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.title: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 1 of its 1 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - project_links (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather
findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 1 of its 1 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - project_links (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 4 read relation(s), 1 were probed live at the gateway (project_links).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 1 of its 1 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - project_links (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 4 read relation(s), 1 were probed live at the gateway (project_links).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

evidence.asserts: the report's progress figure uses the SAME basis project-manager uses - hours-weighted percent-complete - and the basis is legible on screen
evidence.checked: Walked live against the real project SHD-2026-001 (Centrifugal Pump Annual Overhaul, project_id 539e0d9a), with every rendered figure traced back to v_project_items_truth rather than taken from the page's own word. The report renders 'PROGRESS 52% - 3/7 done - HOURS 18 / 33 actual / estimated'. Three different bases could produce a progress number here and they disagree materially, which is exactly why this row exists: counting done items gives 42.9% (3 of 7), comparing hours gives 55.8% (18.4 of 33.0), and weighting each item's pct_complete by its estimated_hours gives 51.5%. The rendered 52% is the WEIGHTED one, rounded - not the count and not the raw hours. project-manager computes its rollup the same way, in code: 'const w = it.estimated_hours || 1; rollup[it.project_id].sum += (it.pct_complete || 0) * w' (project-manager.html:1051-1052). So the two surfaces are not merely close, they are the same formula over the same rows, which is what stops a manager and a report disagreeing about one project. The page also shows the components beside the headline - the 3/7 count and the 18/33 hours - so a reader can see what the 52% is made of instead of having to trust it.

scenarios.oracle: the executive summary's numbers match the detail below them - the classic report defect, where the summary is written once and the detail keeps moving

evidence.asserts: every figure in the executive summary matches the detail beneath it - checked across five independent numbers, not one
evidence.checked: This is the classic report defect - a summary written once while the detail underneath keeps moving - so it was tested with FIVE separate figures rather than one, because a single agreement can be luck. The summary states: 'SHD-2026-001 is 52% complete with 4 scope items remaining', 'PROGRESS 52% - 3/7 done', 'HOURS 18 / 33 actual / estimated', 'BLOCKED 0 scope items', 'DAILY LOGS 3'. Traced to source, v_project_items_truth and v_project_progress_truth for this project return: 7 items with 3 done, therefore 4 remaining; 0 blocked; 33.00 estimated hours against 18.40 actual; and 3 progress logs. All five agree, including the derived one - the 52% is the hours-weighted completion (51.5% rounded), verified separately against project-manager's own formula. The '4 scope items remaining' is the sharpest of these, because it is a DERIVED restatement (7 minus 3) rather than a field, and a stale summary is exactly where such a restatement drifts. On a printed report nobody can refresh to find out which half is current, so this agreement is the whole guarantee.
evidence.value_checked: summary: 52% / 4 remaining / 3 of 7 done / 18 of 33 hours / BLOCKED 0 / DAILY LOGS 3. DB: 7 items, 3 done, 4 remaining, 0 blocked, est 33.00, act 18.40, 3 progress logs. Weighted completion 51.5% -> 52%.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - the component has NO SUBJECT in this state, so there is nothing populated to measure. /workhive/project-report.html (url verified, signed in as Pablo Aguilar) renders 1161 chars and the primary-list probe found listCount 0 across every candidate selector ([class*=row], [class*=card], tb
NOT BANKED - states() blocks the page MAIN THREAD here. Proven: a setTimeout(20000) inside the page NEVER FIRED
findings.detail: THREE attempts, each aborted by the harness at 1800s: once inside a 6-page batch, once as an isolated evaluate on a freshly navigated tab, and once wrapped in an explicit Promise.race against a 20-SECOND setTimeout. That third attempt is the decisive one and it overturns my earlier hypothesis. I had recorded this as "a promise that never settles", the known invisible-hang class on this platform. It is NOT. A pending promise would have lost the race to a 20s timer; that timer NEVER FIRED, and a setTimeout cannot fire while the main thread is busy. So this is a SYNCHRONOUS main-thread block, not an unresolved await - which is a different defect with a different fix, and no amount of timeout wrapping can bound it from inside the page. WHAT THE PROBE DOES THAT COULD CAUSE IT: states() cannot observe loading/skeleton on a settled page so it INDUCES them, and part of that induction is document.dispatchEvent(new Event("DOMContentLoaded")) to re-fire the page loaders. Re-running init on a page whose init is not idempotent is the obvious candidate for an unbounded synchronous loop, and both pages that block are REPORT surfaces that build their content through an orchestrator on init. STATED AS THE LEADING CANDIDATE, NOT AS PROVEN - I have not isolated it, because each attempt costs 1800s of wall clock and I have now spent three. NOTE WHAT IS NOT WRONG: the page itself is healthy. It navigates, renders, and its contrast_wcag, contrast_apca, tap_target_44, w390/w641/w1280_overflow, safe_area and focus_visible rows ALL walked clean today. Only this probe blocks on it. HOW TO RESOLVE WITHOUT BURNING ANOTHER HALF HOUR - do NOT re-run states() on this page. The block is synchronous, so bound it from OUTSIDE the page: run the induction under a Playwright-side timeout (page.evaluate races against the harness, which is what kept killing it) or bisect the induction by calling its steps individually - dispatch the DOMContentLoaded alone first and see whether THAT is what never returns. If it is, the fix is to make the induction not re-dispatch a lifecycle event, or to guard the page init against a second run. Both are cheap once the step is identified. Row stays owed.
findings.observed: 3 x 1800s aborted; a 20s in-page setTimeout never fired, proving main-thread block rather than a pending promise; page navigates and 7 other oracles walked clean

findings.title: OWED, narrowly. axe reports 0 violations and 24 passes over 1 abstention on the populated report - the same near-clean shape as alert-hub (1) and public-feed (3), both of which were banked only AFTER their abstained nodes were identified and measured directly.; That identification was not done on th

false-green-withdrawn 2026-08-07: banked green earlier TODAY on the claim that the APCA row covered axe's abstentions, argued from COUNTS. The exact data-wh-apca membership test refutes it: 4 of 27 abstentions are NOT in the lens's measured set (4 in page content, 0 in shared chrome), so they are judged by neither instrument. Evidence stripped; the row returns to OWED with the exact uncovered list.
findings.detail: DISPOSITIONED BY EXACT SET MEMBERSHIP, NOT BY COUNT - and that change is what makes this entry worth more than the last one. live-state-runner.js stamps every node it measures with data-wh-apca="1" precisely so a caller can ask `el.hasAttribute('data-wh-apca')` per axe abstention (:857). Its own comment states why the count argument can never work: on logbook, loading 4x the content grew the lens denominator 47->219 AND the abstentions 61->249, so the gap WIDENED - the two sets overlap without either containing the other, because the lens scopes to body-minus-shared-chrome by design while axe abstains across the chrome too. PROTOCOL RUN: the lens FIRST (so the stamps exist), then axe over the whole document, then each color-contrast INCOMPLETE node resolved via its axe target selector and asked for the stamp. 0 abstentions were unresolvable on any page, so the intersection is complete rather than sampled. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMED AND WHY IT WAS WRONG: the banked evidence said the 27 incomplete nodes were 'counted as unjudged' and that row 142's APCA (229 measured, 0 inconclusive) covered them, concluding no text was left unjudged. That is the count argument the lens's own comment forbids, and the set test shows 4 nodes in neither instrument's denominator. THE UNCOVERED SET: 4 x .wh-scroll-x table wrappers (text '0') - the scroll CONTAINERS themselves, whose own text belongs to their descendants, so the lens measures the cells and not the wrapper while axe abstains on the wrapper. TO CLOSE: judge those 4 nodes. They are few and characterised, so this is a small concrete task rather than a re-audit - which is the entire value of switching from a count to a set.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 8 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 1167 characters before the refusal and 1167 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than IDENTITY, because this platform has already shipped that exact inversion - a 42501 rendered as 'your session has expired', which sends a signed-IN person to re-authenticate for a problem authentication cannot fix, and 401/403 collapsed into one message so neither audience got a true statement. ZERO of the 16 graded pages made that mistake on this run. utils.js:1607 whIsAuthFailure() is why: it returns FALSE for status 403 with the comment 'authenticated, and refused. Not a session problem', and documents 42501 as insufficient_privilege. That discrimination is holding. HOW THE REFUSAL WAS INDUCED, and why it is the real branch: every Supabase REST read is answered with the body PostgREST actually sends for a row-level-security refusal - HTTP 403 with {"code":"42501","message":"permission denied for table"} - so the page's own error handling takes the same path it would in production. The patch is on window.fetch, NOT page.route, because a warm service worker serves from cache and bypasses route interception; it is installed with addInitScript in a context closed after each page so it cannot leak. NON-WRITING: it makes a READ return 403. THE INJECTION PROVES ITSELF: every intercepted call increments a counter, and a page where the counter is zero is UNGRADED rather than judged. That guard exists because the first version of this prover silently did nothing - a regex written inside a template literal collapsed to one that terminates at its second character, so the init script was a SyntaxError, every read succeeded normally, and the prover reported 'the reads were all refused and the page said nothing' while nothing had been refused at all. Hit counts on this run ranged from 8 to 42 per page. AND THE SIGNAL MUST APPEAR: the same page is read WITHOUT the injection first, and if its ordinary copy already matches the refusal vocabulary the page is UNGRADED - which is exactly what happened to skillmatrix, whose normal text contains a matching phrase. Without that control a page whose everyday copy happens to say 'cannot' would pass for free. THE SYNTHESIS - THIS IS ONE MISSING SURFACE, NOT 15 PAGE BUGS. Of 16 graded pages: 13 said NOTHING AT ALL when every read was refused, 2 showed only a GENERIC error ('Analysis failed, check console'; 'Achievements failed to load.'), and 1 passed. The platform already has the pieces - a central WRITE-failure message and the correct 401-vs-403 discriminator in utils.js - but there is no equivalent on the READ path, so a refused read renders as dashes or blanks with no explanation. On logbook the numbers '516 entries 30 machines 6 open' became '- entries - machines - open' with the body text identical to the character (1107 before and after) and not one word about why. A person cannot tell 'there is no data' from 'the load failed' from 'you are not allowed', and those three call for three different actions. THE FIX IS ONE ADOPTION, not 15 edits: give the read path the same treatment the write path already has. This independently reproduces a finding already recorded as 'the message already exists; the gap is ADOPTION on the read path'. SCOPE: V1, the page as it loads, and READ refusal only - a refused WRITE is a different path with its own central message, and is not claimed here. 5 of the 22 pages are excluded from the sweep because they are public or have no authenticated read to refuse. The walk is NON-WRITING.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_number_labelled.mjs, RE-RUN THIS SESSION - 79 number-bearing elements across the roster, 79 labelled, 0 unlabelled. ★THE DEFINITION IS DELIBERATELY NARROW, because a loose one makes this worthless. A number-bearing element is a LEAF whose trimmed text is numeric-only after stripping currency, separators, % and a unit suffix: '9', '₱1,850,000' and '61%' qualify; '9 open items carried over' does NOT, because it labels itself. And a LABEL is non-numeric text of >=3 characters in the element's own aria-label or title, or in an ANCESTOR's text once the number itself is removed - which is how this platform actually builds stat tiles, with the figure in one span and its name in a sibling. ★THE PROVER CARRIES ITS OWN POSITIVE CONTROL, and every page reports ctl=ok: an element that SHOULD be caught is injected and must be caught. Without that, '0 unlabelled' is indistinguishable from a detector that finds nothing at all - the empty-denominator failure this bank keeps catching. ★AND THE EVIDENCE IS FRESH ON PURPOSE. A clean report from yesterday already existed and I did NOT bank from it: I edited eleven pages this session, so any claim resting on them was staled by my own changes. Re-running a read-only prover is cheaper than reasoning about whether an edit mattered - the same call made for the double-fire run.
